extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public administration; government administrators and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and procedural criteria for designing and applying internal administrative control systems in public organizations, including staffing, delegation, span of control, and cost-effectiveness of control steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control as examination of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Control is the examination of results: to make sure that all operations at all times are carried out in accordance with the plan adopted — with the orders given and with the principles laid down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control compares, discusses and criticizes; it stimulates planning, simplifies and strengthens organization, increases efficiency of command, and facilitates coordination. It may be general or particular and applies at each administrative level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and minimal interference of control systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The best systems of control are carefully planned, simple in their operation, and interfere as little as possible with the normal flow of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within reasonable limits, the best control is the least control. Avoid multiplying clearances and reports that multiply subordinates' work and slow production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcontrol; balance freedom and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Overcontrol should be avoided; there must be a proper balance between subordinate discretion and higher control so as not to destroy the subordinate's ability to get results or impair higher-level effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an undertaking increases in magnitude the importance of higher control increases. Control design must weigh freedom for subordinates against the need for effective higher-level oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Span of control
rubrics_metrics.description: The span of control is the limit within which any one administrator can exercise direct supervision without delegating executive power to subordinates or intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a ‘three-to-six’ rule is sometimes cited (three at top, six at bottom), the workable span depends on operations, environment, organization form, papers handled, decisions required, legal limits, and subordinates' qualifications. Span is determined by volume of control work, not merely by number of people; estimate it by surveying work across the executive's desk and delegating unessential items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete delegation (retention of specified executive powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete delegation is a control device where the superior retains specified executive powers in the operating fields of subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage: allows official scrutiny before decisive steps. Disadvantage: holds up operations when inspection is unnecessary and drains time/energy of high officials, reducing span of control and causing inefficient routing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent delegation to staff units for specialized processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergent delegation is the delegation of specialized processes to staff units (normal for professionalized functions such as accounting, personnel, purchasing, and mechanical operations like stenography and filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized technical offices provide technical control where line administrators have little time. Maintain a proper balance between staff processes and line objectives; avoid staff processes becoming ends in themselves and obscuring basic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reports, conferences, and inspections over clearances when feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports, conferences, and periodic inspection can yield as effective administrative information as clearances and need not block regular activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single report can substitute for numerous case-by-case clearances; scheduled reports/conferences can save time compared with routing most business across an executive's desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness and diminishing returns of control steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Each control step should prevent loss or waste in proportion to its cost; each added control operation is generally worth less than the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate control steps by marginal benefit vs cost (example: first control catches half errors saving $500 at $200 cost; second may be marginal; third may be submarginal). Do not add controls whose cost exceeds their benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls subject to error; excessive control breeds more control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control steps are as subject to error as operating steps; excessive control creates vagueness of responsibility and confusion, increasing the need for more rigid end reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing control to mere initialing of papers in high-volume situations. Keep administrative controls as simple as possible and cut those that delay operating sequences to the bone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan control from function and sequence analysis (three determining factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning of control should start with analysis of the functions and sequences to be controlled; from administrative analysis determine Operating Standard, Normal Deviation, and Control Observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operating Standard: characteristics the finished product must have and permissible tolerance for variation. Normal Deviation: frequency and consequences of deviations exceeding tolerance. Control Observation: ways to observe operations/finished products, who is best qualified to observe, and where they should be located to assure corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplest, most decentralized control that meets standards within tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: The best kind of control for any set of operations is the simplest and most decentralized which will apply the operating standard within the limits of tolerance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in purchasing by competitive bidding the operating standard is acceptance of the lowest bid meeting specifications; tolerance varies with circumstances. Generally better to place fully qualified people in field/divisional jobs and train them than to rely on centralized correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized controls for complex activities must be synchronized and consolidated
rubrics_metrics.description: For large or complex undertakings (e.g., housing, flood control, power development), controls must be more elaborate and highly specialized, involving experts from engineering, economic, legal, social, psychological, and political fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide adequate review of plans by proper professionals; synchronize and consolidate specialized control operations; controls should be specific and expressed in definite standards. If a plan meets standards it should generally be passed even if framed differently than a reviewer would have done it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplicate administration and repetition of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplication or repetition of control activities (multiple units with overlapping jurisdictions or repeated work by units) can cause administrative paralysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control mechanisms should be planned to produce definite results in the simplest, shortest way. Prefer reports and inspections to clearances where effective; schedule clearances and reviews and subject them to time limits; examine technical phases concurrently and use a coordinator to synthesize opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls for unstandardized executive work: train in policy and classify subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Where work is unstandardized and each day differs, the best control is thorough education in over-all policy and a common-sense classification of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A survey will often reveal recurrent subjects; classification helps subordinates perceive what to bring to the chief's attention and what they may dispose of independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign control operations by practical span and provide executive assistants when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Control operations should be assigned to fit the specific situation (practical span), not theoretical responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executives absent part-time should not be asked to sign all division correspondence or clear requisitions; an overburdened administrator should have sufficient executive assistants to collect information and relieve minor affairs so decisions can be made rapidly and thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control should begin with the job itself; place qualified people and encourage voluntary adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who does the job should know the standards by which he will be judged and should be trained to apply them as he goes along.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many types of work the most effective control is obtained by encouraging voluntary adherence to a standard rather than centralized correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each operating step and control step must have a definite purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Each task in an administrative sequence should contribute positively to the desired end; each operating step should have a definite purpose, and each control step should prevent loss or waste proportional to its cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure value of control steps by observable results with and without them; eliminate steps without a clear, cost-justified purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidate controls and aim for high-quality, low-quantity control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control operations should be consolidated and made as effective as possible after careful study of operating methods, objectives, deviations, and observation techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient procedure is simple procedure with short administrative sequences. Controls should be high in quality and low in quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Service oversight authority and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Civil Service Commission should have power to demand any departmental records pertaining to personnel matters and ample power to enforce its decisions; where functions are decentralized to departments, the Commission should have authority comparable to the General Accounting Office in financial matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority supports centralized control even when operations are decentralized and is necessary to enforce standards and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine decentralized operation with centralized control in personnel matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized operation combined with centralized control can be no more dangerous in personnel handling than in financial matters; decentralization is not a new experiment in some agencies and a career service can exist with departmental independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow departments operational flexibility while retaining central standards and oversight to prevent abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use departmental working agreements to tailor specifications and reduce delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Working agreements between departments and the central commission assure line agencies of specifications suited to their needs and eliminate delay caused by negotiation over details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments can deviate somewhat from central tendencies in expressing qualifications when they prepare exams; this avoids overly narrow qualification sequences required by central agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit applicant volume by charging a reasonable application fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Charge a fee for Civil Service applications (suggested $2.00–$5.00) to limit the volume of applications and finance Civil Service work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees exclude applicants not seriously interested or not reasonably sure they can meet qualifications; stricter grading for professional positions is a parallel expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralize grading of specialized examinations with safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralize grading of specialized examinations to departments, particularly when they prepared the exams, to reduce delays and permit more subject-matter–oriented testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate safeguards are required to ensure impartiality: raters must certify they are not acquainted with the applicant except by official interview results. Departmental registers should be reviewed by the Commission and administered by its Certification Division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish veterans' preference and apportionment; determine standing by merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative standing in appointments should be determined solely by merit; veterans' preference and state apportionment can clutter registers with underqualified applicants and unfairly favor some applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veterans' preference tends to produce repeated certifications and build prejudice; apportionment by states is a relic favoring those from certain states and can disadvantage more qualified candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralize classification with central manuals and audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Give departmental classifiers authority commensurate with skill and experience while the Civil Service Commission maintains control by issuing a standard manual and conducting periodic classification audits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audits should correct erroneous allocations; departments may refer doubtful classifications to the Commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorize departments to approve status changes with post-approval control
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow departments to determine eligibility for transfer or promotion once position qualifications are established, subject to post-approval by the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Commission fails to post-approve personnel actions within a prescribed framework, the employee would revert to original status; this preserves departmental flexibility while retaining central oversight.
